item.title: My modes of working with agents
item.description:
Recently I wrote about how I use agents for software work. In this follow-up, I want to dive into more details of my workflow. I’ll walk through three modes of working I use, and how I pick between them. Each mode has a different level of involvement from me.

You don’t need to read the full previous post, but you should know that I use a “brain session”, which is just a Claude Code/Codex/Pi instance that is capable of launching more instances. For more details, my full setup is public in brain-public.

To make my descriptions more concrete, this post follows the story of my (imaginary) friend Pascal, who is opening a tech-forward bakery called Boolangerie. Since I work with computers, obviously I’m the friend he calls for anything computer, but luckily he pays me with fresh croissants!

Worker mode

🥐 At Boolangerie...

My friend Pascal has the bakery almost ready to go: he opens in a week!

He needs a domain name, email, website, and a social media strategy, quickly.

I open my main brain session, and prompt it:

The brain session creates one new session for each of the tasks, and primes it with some context it already has: Pascal had sent me an email with some pictures for the website, so they have some context on Boolangerie. Each of those sessions is what we call a “worker”: they’re a Claude Code or a Codex or a Pi agent.

Each of the workers suggests a plan of action, and I go to each and review, and from then on do a normal interactive session with it. I spend the next few days switching between these workers until the work is done.

When to use this

It’s a one-off task, or the first task of a new project. I find I can keep track of up to 5 workers like this, but if doing it long enough I typically feel AI brain fry. If you have more than 3, I’d recommend moving to the manager mode.

Manager mode

🥐 At Boolangerie...

The launch has been a success! Pascal has more customers than he can handle, and he’s asking for my help managing it.

He wants a user area on the website for regular customers, with the ability to order for pickup. Every time he speaks to me he has more requests: we need customers to be able to select pick-up time slots, we need to send them reminders when they pre-order, we need to set up a loyalty stamp, we need them to have order history, and they need to be able to pay online.

Ah and the existing customers have started complaining about missing information on the website.

I open my brain session, and prompt it:

Then I have a “manager worker” that I can interact with. This manager is in charge of keeping track of what needs doing, and keeping me informed on the status of tasks. It’s a smart ticket manager, which also helps me break down the tasks. I tell it to spin up some workers to do these initial tasks:

I switch from worker to worker and move the tasks along. Before I finish them, Pascal comes in with the next requests. I go to the manager, break the problems down into tasks, and get new workers for all of them.

This is too much information for me all at once, so the manager is keeping me sane by helping me select where to put my attention. The manager has a dashboard to help me:

The dashboard tells me which worker I need to look at, so my day is still context switching between the multiple workers.

When to use this

Whenever you have an ongoing project that will have multiple tasks.

This severely alleviates the cognitive load when doing many small tasks: you still keep both high and low-level decisions, but you’re released from keeping track of everything at once.

I got the dashboard idea from Thariq Shihipar’s episode on the Latent Space podcast. Everything else in this post is agnostic to the harness you use, but the dashboard is specifically using Claude Code.

PM + Tech Lead mode

🥐 At Boolangerie...

Pascal has been keeping the staff shifts on a whiteboard, and managing his stock in a notebook. Last week one of the bakers thought he was off and didn’t show up, and on Saturday they ran out of flour!

I’ll build him a simple web app to help keep track of stock and shifts. My day job has been busy recently, so I can’t give it much attention, but the app is only for Pascal’s staff. If it breaks, the worst case is they fall back to the whiteboard and notebook for a day 🤷‍♂️.

I open my brain session, and prompt it:

This is the most complicated setup, and it’s also the most hands-off. I speak only with the “project manager worker”, whose job is to orchestrate the work. The “tech lead worker” is in charge of making decisions on which tech to use, how to break the problem down into tasks, and verifying the work of the other workers. The PM ensures the work moves along, but the tech lead is making the actual decisions.

This animation shows how I interact with the PM:

In this setup, I’m not interacting with any of the workers directly. I set direction, like a CEO would in a real company, and unblock the workers as needed (need new context, access to a website, installing some tool, etc). This is the most hands-off I work, but even in this case I do keep track of which PRs are being opened and usually set a requirement that I need to review them. I find this to be a very good way to reliably set up long tasks (think 5+ hours without my interaction).

Doing it like this allows me to work on multiple projects at the same time, without really exhausting me. I’m abstracting myself from the low-level decisions completely, but am still in charge of the high-level ones.

When to use this

Whenever you have a big task with lots of parts, with low cost of failure. Internal tools and greenfield projects fit this. I find having an Opus 5.5 for a tech lead makes the outcome quite reliable, because it’s incredibly thorough at verifying the work. But I haven’t been brave enough to use these techniques for products that are actually used by a big audience.

What’s next?

The ideas presented above can be tweaked to fit whatever work styles you prefer. I made up the roles like project manager and tech lead for concepts that make sense to me, but you could easily add a QA worker or a product manager worker, or whatever else you can think of. You can and should customize it to your world.

However, changing the roles only gets you so far. In all the examples above, we have a single developer looking over all of those agents, and if there’s a 2nd person who wants to work with the same agents, they just can’t.

The next step comes from scaling the humans: you want a setup where your colleagues are using the same agents as you. People have been calling these software factories. If you want to learn more, check out warp.dev’s post, or reach out to me because I’ve built one at Unitary.

Close

This post describes some ways of working I’ve been using myself, and they cover a range of autonomy for the agents. Choosing the appropriate mode for each task is not a simple problem, but I’d summarize the decision as a trade-off between speed and robustness of development: if bugs have low real-world impact, prioritize speed. If you’re flying a plane, any bug puts lives at risk, so be very hands-on. If you’re doing a game for your friends, bugs are at worst a minor annoyance. Most work falls somewhere in the middle.

In practice, I’m generally working with a mix of those modes:

As in the previous post, you can check the details of how I’m implementing these modes of work in my public repo, but don’t copy them directly. Instead, I recommend you take inspiration from it and make your own skills that fit your working style.

item.title: How I use agents for work
item.description:
I’ve had both friends and colleagues ask how I’m using agents for work. It’s easier to show than explain. Click the buttons in this animation to experience my typical morning:

The above is genuinely how I work nowadays. Most days I’m working on 3-10 tasks in parallel. The trick isn’t the agents or the harness. It’s that, by the time I ask, they already have the context.

If you write software and want to get more out of your agents, this is how I’ve set this up. My full setup is publicly available here, though it won’t make much sense without this post.

Context is everything

It doesn’t matter how good the model is: if it doesn’t get the correct information, it won’t accomplish its task. My job these days is not to write code, but rather to ensure that my agents have access to the right context.

So let’s talk about where my agents are getting their context from. This plot compares the sources before/after I had this setup described in this post, as well as its impact on my productivity:

My Second Brain

The most important piece of context in my setup is the “second brain”. This brain is simply a text store where all agents are saving important information after every session. This turned out to be the most impactful source of context after I set up this system. In the first few weeks there’s not much there so it’s not super useful, but as it becomes populated the agents start relying on it more and more.

In practice, this is an Obsidian vault (that is, a bunch of markdown files), the capability to index it (I’m using qmd), and some rules to get all Claude Code sessions to write to it.

Meetings

I have very few meetings myself, but find that the context in them is typically very important. I find it hard to remember all the details of what we speak about in a meeting, but agents excel at that. Despite it not being a very prominent source of information in the plot above, I’d rank its importance as 2nd only to the brain itself.

In my setup I’m using Krisp to record/transcribe meetings, and then use its MCP service to pull them into my vault. Fortunately for me I work remotely, so I know all meetings will go through my computer; if you work in person this might be hard to replicate.

Logs

For bug fixing, logs are the most important source. If the agents can see the bugs happening, then you don’t need to explain what’s actually happening.

I’ve been using Datadog, which also has an MCP service. I find that the agents sometimes use Kubernetes commands directly also, for cases where something is happening live rather than a retrospective investigation.

Communications

Then there’s the messaging platforms and docs. I use Slack to communicate with colleagues, Gmail for customers, and Notion as a wiki. All of these have pretty good MCP connections. I find agents are surprisingly good at searching Slack in particular, they often find things I couldn’t myself.

Linking them together

As an example, a customer asked me to make some changes to how our code was matching names. This was one of many requests in a call with them, a small change for which I didn’t memorize all the details. After the meeting, the summary and tasks were added to the brain.

The next day I started an agent with “make the changes to ignore middle names like we talked in yesterday’s call”, and the agent went to work. The agent knew the summarized information was second-hand, so went straight to the source call and found all the details. It turns out the rules were overly simplified in the summary that was saved in the brain! They were complex: first/last name alternative spellings were meant to be flagged for human review, when completely different they should be rejected, and only when they completely match (except for the middle name which would be ignored) should they be accepted.

Not only did I not tell the agent all of this, but I’d forgotten all of those details. I checked later and they did match the agreed rules during the 1 minute or so that we discussed in the call. I didn’t give the agent the rules, I just made sure it could find them!

A typical work day

Before standup

I open up a new session and call a skill: an agent summarizes what I did yesterday, so I have an easy reference to read from during the standup. I find having some writing to look at helps me not forget topics I want to talk about. I also found—as I started doing more tasks per day—that I kept forgetting some things I had done.

After standup

Typically in a standup I’ll talk about what I’m doing today, and colleagues make requests of me. So after the call I have a todo list for the day, and I unleash my agents! I do this not only for programming tasks, but for almost all tasks: if I need to send a plot to Alice with the week’s data, I open a session so I don’t forget it. Each task has one dedicated agent.

Note: this is the same animation I used in the intro of this post.

During the day

Most of my time is context switching between the multiple tasks. I check what an agent needs from me, do what it takes to unblock it, and move on to the next agent. In practice I’m micromanaging all these agents, I’m choosing designs, I’m confirming bugs, I’m running commands myself and reporting results. Each agent gets a bit of my attention, instead of one task getting all of it.

To make it a bit easier to manage, I use tmux with some Claude Code hooks that change the tmux session name to include a 🔔 for the sessions that need me.

Wrapping up tasks

When each agent finishes, they are “collected” and “torn down”. This just means that they write up a summary of the session (including what new information they learned) into the brain, and then clean up all the temporary files they left. This is often git worktrees, or some scripts that will never be needed again.

Without this step, none of the above would work. These summaries are the most important part of the brain setup! They’re what make the “pre-standup” skill work, and then everything else from there.

I typically have one “brain” session which is in charge of doing this, and there are some skills on how to do it since it’s such a common process.

During the week

Those systems described above all work on a daily basis. However, projects don’t typically work at day-scale, so I have a few more tricks:

  1. Backlog: In the vault, there’s a backlog file. The sessions know to write there whenever there’s some follow-up work that will need doing. It doesn’t get done automatically, but it’s there so we can get to it when appropriate.
  2. Weekly goals: When planning what to do each day, it’s useful to have goals that are one level higher. Therefore each week I plan out weekly goals (usually together with my team), and then when planning each day I have an easy reference point for what to prioritize.
  3. Dreaming: All the sessions store what went wrong in their summary. Every now and then, I have an agent go over these problems and address them. They’re typically changes to the setup itself. One example: my machine has ls aliased to colorls, and therefore the scripts Claude made with ls broke in unexpected ways. All agents were having to run into the issue and work around it, until one dreaming session noticed it and decided to put that note in CLAUDE.md.

Prior art and inspiration

Nothing in here is revolutionary, this is just how I’ve been working these days. The concept of the “2nd brain” was quite popular on Twitter and was introduced to me by Matt Camp at Unitary. I took the general ideas and adjusted them to my setup and ways of working.

I’m not aware of any general framework doing all of this automatically right now. I think it likely is possible to do one, but I find it hard to adopt other people’s workflows precisely as they use it. If you’re like me, I think a custom setup like described here is the only way to go.

Conclusion

Everything in this post is about context. Having the right context allows you to live one level of abstraction higher. I don’t promise that working like this leads to tasks getting done faster than manually, but it will allow you to do more tasks in the same time. With this workflow, I’m working on 3-10 tasks simultaneously at any given time.

I’m sharing my setup as a repo here. It includes the skills I use and a little bit on how to use them. It also includes more systems than those described here. I’m planning to write some follow-up posts: how I manage agents, when to trust agents, and forcing agents to follow my instructions (hint: this is just pawl).

I don’t recommend you install those specific skills, but rather take ideas from it and start building your own. Have an agent read over it and recommend one or two ideas to start using in your workflows.

We’re back at the vi configs era, but now we “config” them in English!
